variants.title: Sweep length and depth
variants.context: A defensible long-context evaluation names the behavior, sweeps length and evidence depth, raises interference, and then publishes the tested frontier. One long prompt proves one point.
variants.prompt: A team has run one 180,000 token prompt, seen a correct answer, and written that the model supports 180K. Put the evaluation steps in order.

items.text: Add similar entities, stale versions, and contradictions, then record whether the answer cites the controlling source.
Separate the behaviors under test, because single retrieval, multi-document reasoning, and aggregation need different ground truth.
Publish the slice results and the tested frontier without averaging adjacent cells into untested regions.
Place equivalent evidence near the beginning, middle, and end at several context lengths with deterministic seeds.

variants.hint: One placement at one length is a single cell of the grid.
variants.explanation: Position belongs in the claim. A passing point test says nothing about the depths and lengths that were never run.

variants.title: Sweep length and depth
variants.context: A defensible long-context evaluation names the behavior, sweeps length and evidence depth, raises interference, and then publishes the tested frontier. One long prompt proves one point.
variants.prompt: A contract assistant must find an exception clause that can appear anywhere in a filing. Put the steps that build its evaluation in order.

items.text: Report each length and depth cell separately and state the largest region that actually passed.
Declare that the behavior is single retrieval with a citation to the controlling clause, not free summarization.
Add superseded versions of the clause and clauses from sibling contracts so the model must pick the controlling one.
Insert the same clause at ten, fifty, and ninety percent depth across 8K, 32K, and 64K token inputs, repeating each cell.

variants.hint: Which step decides what ground truth even means here?
variants.explanation: The behavior contract chooses the scorer, so it is named before any case is generated.

variants.title: Sweep length and depth
variants.context: A defensible long-context evaluation names the behavior, sweeps length and evidence depth, raises interference, and then publishes the tested frontier. One long prompt proves one point.
variants.prompt: A support product must summarize an entire ticket history, and the current suite hides one fact in the middle of the input. Put the steps in order.

items.text: Add contradicting older messages and near-duplicate tickets so omissions and unsupported additions become visible.
Publish coverage and consistency per length, and mark the untested lengths as untested.
Spread the required points across the whole input at several total lengths and repeat with fixed seeds.
Name the behavior as global aggregation, which needs required-point coverage rather than one hidden string.

variants.hint: A single hidden string is not evidence of global use.
variants.explanation: Aggregation is scored on required-point coverage, factual consistency, omissions, and unsupported additions.

variants.title: Gate the operating frontier
variants.context: The usable window is the largest tested region where every release-critical slice passes its declared quality, evidence-use, and latency floors. Floors are set before candidate results are read, and any failing slice blocks.
variants.prompt: A team is preparing the release review for a long-context assistant and wants to know how large a window it may claim. Put the gate steps in order.

items.text: Block the release if any slice carries a blocker, and otherwise grant a bounded canary.
Publish the tested maximum context as the claim boundary instead of the accepted API maximum.
Evaluate every length and depth slice against those floors rather than the grid average.
Declare the task success floor, the citation recall floor, and the p95 latency budget before looking at results.
Collect the blockers per slice, separating task success, citation recall, and latency failures.

variants.hint: Floors are declared before the candidate numbers are visible.
variants.explanation: The accepted window says the request fits. The supported frontier is what passed quality, grounding, latency, and cost together.

variants.title: Gate the operating frontier
variants.context: The usable window is the largest tested region where every release-critical slice passes its declared quality, evidence-use, and latency floors. Floors are set before candidate results are read, and any failing slice blocks.
variants.prompt: At 64K tokens the p95 completion latency is 7.4 seconds against a 6 second budget, while task success and citation recall pass everywhere. Put the steps in order.

items.text: Record the 64K slice blocker as latency above budget, leaving its quality metrics marked as passing.
State the supported frontier at the largest length that passed every floor together.
Confirm the 6 second p95 budget was part of the predeclared gate and not adjusted after the run.
Check each slice individually so the passing 8K and 32K cells do not absorb the 64K result.
Block the 64K claim while allowing the shorter tested lengths to proceed to a bounded canary.

variants.hint: Latency is a floor of its own, not something quality can offset.
variants.explanation: Quality, grounding, latency, and cost must pass together, so a fast-enough shorter window can ship while the long one does not.

variants.title: Gate the operating frontier
variants.context: The usable window is the largest tested region where every release-critical slice passes its declared quality, evidence-use, and latency floors. Floors are set before candidate results are read, and any failing slice blocks.
variants.prompt: Every slice in the grid passes its floors and the team asks to enable the new window for all traffic immediately. Put the steps in order.

items.text: Record that there are no blockers, so the outcome is a canary rather than a block.
Claim only the tested maximum context and leave untested lengths outside the contract.
Confirm no individual length and depth slice fell below task success, citation recall, or latency.
Attach abort thresholds and a rollback target to the bounded rollout.
Verify the floors were declared before the run and that both candidates used the same protocol.

variants.hint: What does a clean offline grid actually buy?
variants.explanation: Passing offline evidence earns a bounded canary with abort thresholds, not an unmonitored global rollout.

variants.title: Size the matrix
variants.context: The matrix builder creates one case per context length, evidence depth, and repeat, so the case count is the product of those three. The slice count is the product of lengths and depths alone.
variants.prompt: A matrix builder is given three context lengths, five evidence depths, and three repeats per cell. How many evaluation cases does it produce?
variants.hint: Each repeat is its own case with its own seed and case ID.
variants.explanation: The case count is lengths times depths times repeats, because a case exists for every combination.

mistakes.feedback: That is the slice count; each slice is still run for every repeat.
You added the three dimensions instead of multiplying them.

variants.title: Size the matrix
variants.context: The matrix builder creates one case per context length, evidence depth, and repeat, so the case count is the product of those three. The slice count is the product of lengths and depths alone.
variants.prompt: A team sweeps four context lengths and five evidence depths with two repeats per cell. The coverage check asks how many distinct length-by-depth slices must be present. How many slices is that?
variants.hint: A slice is a length paired with a depth, however many times it was rerun.
variants.explanation: Coverage is asserted on the set of length and depth pairs, so repeats narrow uncertainty inside a slice rather than adding slices.

mistakes.feedback: That is the case count including both repeats, not the number of distinct slices.
You added lengths and depths instead of multiplying them.

variants.title: Size the matrix
variants.context: The matrix builder creates one case per context length, evidence depth, and repeat, so the case count is the product of those three. The slice count is the product of lengths and depths alone.
variants.prompt: An existing matrix covers three context lengths, five evidence depths, and three repeats. The team adds a fourth context length with the same depths and repeats. How many new cases does that add?
variants.hint: Only the cells that did not exist before are new.
variants.explanation: Adding one length adds its depths times its repeats, which is why widening the length sweep costs more than adding a repeat.

mistakes.feedback: That is the number of new slices, before the repeats are counted.
That is the size of the whole matrix after the addition, not the number added.

variants.title: Match the scorer to the behavior
variants.context: Answer overlap alone can reward an unsupported guess. Single retrieval, multi-document reasoning, and aggregation each need a different ground truth and scorer, and the expected evidence IDs travel with the case.
variants.prompt: A product must summarize a long incident history, and the current suite scores it by checking whether one hidden sentence appears in the output.
options: Score required-point coverage, omissions, and unsupported additions with evidence spread across the input.
Replace the check with answer overlap against a reference summary written by one reviewer.
Keep the hidden sentence check and raise the number of input lengths it runs at.
optionFeedback: Aggregation promises coverage and consistency, so the scorer must look for required points and unsupported additions.
Overlap with one reference rewards phrasing and cannot separate an omission from a wording difference.
More lengths repeat the same narrow recall probe and still say nothing about global use.
variants.hint: Which promised behavior does one hidden string fail to exercise?
variants.explanation: One hidden needle is a positional smoke test. Aggregation needs evidence distributed across the whole input.

variants.title: Match the scorer to the behavior
variants.context: Answer overlap alone can reward an unsupported guess. Single retrieval, multi-document reasoning, and aggregation each need a different ground truth and scorer, and the expected evidence IDs travel with the case.
variants.prompt: A policy assistant answers from several documents that disagree, because an older version was never withdrawn.
options: Score citation count, treating more cited sources as stronger grounding for the answer.
Score only the final answer string against the expected value for the case.
Score the answer and each required supporting fact, checking that cited passages entail it.
optionFeedback: Counting citations rewards volume and cannot tell the controlling source from the withdrawn one.
A correct final string can come from the superseded document, which is the failure being tested.
Multi-document reasoning is scored on the answer and every required fact, including which version controls.
variants.hint: The failure here is which document was used, not what the answer said.
variants.explanation: Multi-document cases need per-fact scoring and conflicts that force version, authority, or effective-date reasoning.

variants.title: Match the scorer to the behavior
variants.context: Answer overlap alone can reward an unsupported guess. Single retrieval, multi-document reasoning, and aggregation each need a different ground truth and scorer, and the expected evidence IDs travel with the case.
variants.prompt: A lookup feature returns one value from a long filing, and the filing contains three subsidiaries with nearly identical names.
options: Score by string overlap with the reference so near-miss answers still earn partial credit.
Accept any normalized answer that matches one of the three similar entity records.
Require the correct value plus its stable document identifier, and track similar-name false positives.
optionFeedback: Partial credit for a near miss hides a retrieval failure behind a similar-looking string.
Accepting any of the three similar records is exactly the confusion the distractors were built to catch.
Single retrieval is scored on exact correctness plus the source identifier, with false positives tracked separately.
variants.hint: What distinguishes the right subsidiary from the plausible one?
variants.explanation: Single retrieval requires the source span or stable identifier, and distractor false positives are counted on their own.

variants.title: Sort the run record
variants.context: Every long-context result stores five record groups: the candidate that ran, the input that was built, the retrieval state that supplied sources, the scoring protocol that judged it, and the operational cost of the run.
variants.prompt: A stored long-context result lists five fields. Match each field to the record group it belongs to.

pairs.label: Candidate
pairs.detail: Model version, tokenizer, system prompt, and generation parameters.

pairs.label: Input
pairs.detail: Document order, truncation policy, evidence positions, and random seeds.

pairs.label: Retrieval
pairs.detail: Index and embedding version, filters, top-k policy, and returned source IDs.

pairs.label: Scoring
pairs.detail: Expected facts, citation contract, metric version, and human-review policy.

pairs.label: Operations
pairs.detail: Input and output tokens, time to first token, p95 latency, and cost.

variants.hint: Ask whether the field describes what ran, what it read, where sources came from, how it was judged, or what it cost.
variants.explanation: Sorting the record this way lets a reviewer name the exact thing that changed between two runs.

variants.title: Sort the run record
variants.context: Every long-context result stores five record groups: the candidate that ran, the input that was built, the retrieval state that supplied sources, the scoring protocol that judged it, and the operational cost of the run.
variants.prompt: Two runs of the same suite disagree and five details were never stored. Match each missing detail to its record group.

pairs.label: Candidate
pairs.detail: The serving configuration the request was routed through.

pairs.label: Input
pairs.detail: The source snapshot the long prompt was built from.

pairs.label: Retrieval
pairs.detail: The reranker and chunk boundaries used before assembly.

pairs.label: Scoring
pairs.detail: The judge prompt and the adjudication result for disputed cases.

pairs.label: Operations
pairs.detail: The retry count and the refusals observed during the run.

variants.hint: Chunk boundaries belong with the component that produced the sources.
variants.explanation: A missing identity turns a reproducible measurement into an argument about which run was right.

variants.title: Sort the run record
variants.context: Every long-context result stores five record groups: the candidate that ran, the input that was built, the retrieval state that supplied sources, the scoring protocol that judged it, and the operational cost of the run.
variants.prompt: A reviewer asks five questions about last night's grid. Match each question to the record group that answers it.

pairs.label: Candidate
pairs.detail: Which tool definitions were available while these answers were produced?

pairs.label: Input
pairs.detail: At which depth was the evidence placed in this case?

pairs.label: Retrieval
pairs.detail: Which source IDs did the index actually return?

pairs.label: Scoring
pairs.detail: Which metric version decided that this citation counted?

pairs.label: Operations
pairs.detail: How long did the ninety-fifth percentile completion take?

variants.hint: Two of these questions are about the prompt that was built, not the model that read it.
variants.explanation: Every question a release review asks should resolve to one stored record group rather than a rerun.
